title: Northwest Minnesota group searches for the elusive Bigfoot
excerpt: They say looking for Sasquatch has brought a whole new dimension to enjoying the outdoors.
content:
Several years ago, Nathan Kniefel decided to go winter camping in Hubbard County, in northwestern Minnesota. It was a cold December day in the woods, but during the course of his stay, he saw something that would send another type of chill up his spine: large footprints that looked very much like a human’s but were too big to be from a man.

Kniefel’s thoughts raced and he remembered the documentary films he’d seen about the legendary Sasquatch — otherwise known as Bigfoot. Could one of the creatures have crossed his campground?

It wouldn’t have been out of the ordinary, he thought, since northern Minnesota has attracted a lot of stories over the decades about Bigfoot sightings. There’s even a northern Minnesota town — Remer, population 381 — dubbed “Home of Bigfoot” for the propensity of alleged creature sightings in the area stretching back to the early 1900s. Every July, the town hosts Bigfoot Days, a community celebration centered around the elusive ape-like beast.

“I’m not going to sit here and say I’ve seen Bigfoot,” Kniefel told the Grand Forks Herald. Nonetheless, seeing the prints and tracking them in the woods was a game-changer for him. If nothing else, even considering the possibility the prints were from a Sasquatch made the camping experience a little more intriguing and a lot more fun.

Kniefel’s experience in the woods prompted him to form the Northern Minnesota Bigfoot Organization , and soon a few friends joined the venture.

Today, the three team members — Kniefel, founder and researcher; Brent Ekstrom, expedition lead and indigenous guide; and Christopher Mathisen, chief financial officer, all from Bemidji and the surrounding area — gather several times a year to visit and investigate areas of alleged Bigfoot sightings in northern Minnesota. They call their outings “expeditions” and said tracking the creature of folklore and legend brings purpose to their adventures, although the more immediate benefit is just being outdoors, traversing the Minnesota woods and enjoying all that Mother Nature has to offer in the North Star State.

Expedition in the outdoors

Kniefel said his solo camping trip from the winter of 2019 changed the course of his life and made him more aware of his surroundings when in the backcountry.

Of that experience, he said once he found a clearing to pitch his tent, he noticed large footprints nearby. Intrigued, he tried replicating the stride length but couldn't. He put his hand in the snow next to a print and took a picture. He said his hand is about 8 inches, but the footprint was twice that long.

“They were pretty much where I was camping,” he said. “These prints were huge.”

He noticed the print track led into the woods. He followed, noticing another set of large footprints had come close to the other as if there had been two creatures that had walked side by side. His findings didn’t scare him off.

“I actually camped there for the night. Of course, nothing happened,” he said.

Kniefel never encountered the creature that made the footprints. However, he did send pictures to his friends, telling them, “This is crazy. I might have actually seen Bigfoot tracks.”

Ever since, the friends have been researching Bigfoot sightings in northwest Minnesota. It’s not a full-time job, but they do it when they have time. They say the venture has brought another level to their outdoor and camping experiences.

“We’ve always gone out and kind of roughed it up,” Kniefel said. “We’d sleep under the stars, sleep on tarps. Not to say we were making it miserable on purpose but we’ve taken joy in it; as rough as we could get, we just love that.”

Ekstrom said it’s been fun going afield, leaving daily duties behind.

“I think it’s really nice to get out there and only focus on what's in front of you — and you can control a lot of what’s going in front of you when you’re setting up camp, when you’re cooking, when you’re hanging out around the fire,” he said. “It’s a lot easier to focus on that and prepare for the expedition knowing that we're all centered around one thing: finding Bigfoot.”

The elusive Sasquatch

The three team members are only a few of the countless people over time who claim to have encountered Bigfoot's tracks, heard its howling or found its fur. The first widely recognized modern sighting of the unknowable creature is from 1958 in Humboldt County, California — although bipedal creature sightings have historically been reported since the late 1700s. Sasquatch reports have occurred in most U.S. states, including Minnesota, such as the following from Nov. 27, 2011.

A husband and wife were traveling on Highway 7 in Itasca County when they claimed to have seen a figure they at first thought was a man near the side of the road. The husband told his wife, who was driving, to slow down. As she did, and their vehicle drew closer, the figure started to cross the road in front of them. It was then that they could see the bipedal creature was something else entirely.

The man, reporting the incident to the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization — the first and largest group of its kind that compiles Bigfoot sightings across North America — described the creature as “covered in dark brown fur,” 6 to 7 feet tall, with “a broad nose” and with “little hair on its forehead or cheeks. Its feet were covered with long hair like a Clydesdale horse that trailed on the pavement as it crossed. Its chest had welts that I reasoned were from insect bites. It had long muscular arms and when it reached the other side of the road [it] swung his arms and leaped the entire ditchway.” It also walked with an “unusual” gait.

The man, who said he’s hunted the Minnesota forests for decades, ended the report by saying he was “very well trained” in recognizing different types of wildlife but the creature he and his wife saw that day “was no human in a suit.”

It is one of many reports filed of strange creature sightings in Itasca County. Other places where people claim to have either heard or saw something they attribute to the monster include Bemidji, Duluth and the area surrounding Leech Lake Reservation, among many others.

North Dakota also has reports of Bigfoot sightings. One of the most popular was from a man who claims to have tracked the creature in the winter of 2017 in Ellendale. “Someone saw him, and he left behind a trail and tracks,” resident Christopher Bauer told WDAY at the time.

As with other alleged Bigfoot findings, there have been the naysayers. A question that has arisen among skeptics is this: If there really is a Bigfoot — or a Loch Ness Monster or Pepie, Minnesota's version of Nessie that supposedly haunts Lake Pepin — why has there been no concrete evidence that proves its existence?

Images of the supposed Sasquatch are often blurred, grainy or too far away to determine the true character of the creature. Even with today’s technology, the existence of Sasquatch has never been conclusively investigated and confirmed.

Also, faking images and plaster casts of large footprints are not out of the realm of possibility, and some have proven to be deceptions.

Despite the lack of crucial evidence, the lore of Bigfoot continues. For members of the NMBO, there’s a simple reason why evidence is lacking. The species of creature, whatever it might be, is just smart enough to elude photographic and other evidence just as it has done for a long time.

“I think he’s the greatest ape of apes,” said Mathisen. “I believe he’s more intelligent than we like to give him credit for; he’s just very elusive. I think he’s way smarter than we fathom and that’s why he’s so difficult” to photograph.

Kniefel, who studied ecology and evolutionary biology at Minnesota State University Mankato, said if he had to guess what Bigfoot is, “I just assume it’s an animal of some kind, an undiscovered animal. I mean, new species are found every day.

“In the United States, we have some pretty expansive, remote areas. If you look at the population density of northern Minnesota, it’s pretty sparse. ...

“If there is an ape creature in the woods, I don’t necessarily think he’s wandering around Bemidji, Minnesota. But who knows. We are right on the border of Canada and it gets more remote the farther north you go.”

Ekstrom said that in Native culture, there are many tales of cryptids — including the wendigo, a cannibalistic humanoid monster — that have ties to the human element. Bigfoot is only one of them.

“So I think in my community, we see Bigfoot as maybe a lost, wandering soul. Or maybe even an ancestor coming back to talk with us, coming to relay something to us,” he said. “Maybe the finding of Bigfoot is the soul-searching we do when we’re out in the woods.”

The team members will continue their search for the elusive creature. Maybe one day technology will catch up with the legend.

“Sometimes it’s not the destination, it’s the journey,” Kniefel said.
